Summary

GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-V4-Flash on 2×DGX Spark — full comparison (15 configs)

This is the updated consolidating post of our GLM-5.3-Flash / DeepSeek-V4-Flash on-prem benchmark series on two DGX Spark GB10 boxes (2×128 GB unified, TP2 over RoCE). Since the previous consolidation we added one fully measured config: D-FP4L (nvidia’s official GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local, NVFP4 quantization-aware distillation 1.0, served on the eugr spark-vllm-docker b12x recipe, vLLM 0.1.dev21830+g8244d1c44.d20261015). TensorFold fp8 (G647) trades single-stream 4k-decode (31.8–55.8) for the strongest 0-depth c2/c4 decode (65.9–69.3 / 59.6–59.7). Canada W4A16 decodes flat and low (18–43) at every cell — marlin W4A16 without the draft-acceptance advantage. G644a/G (q4) still own the deepest single-stream cells (58–74), which is exactly why their q4-era tg numbers must not be compared against fp8 rows. D-FP4L is flat-low (25–42) like Canada, but its native MTP n=5 acceptance is strongly prompt-typed: 81.6% on structured prompts (single-stream ~53–54 t/s there, above T) vs ~30% code / ~20–35% filler — the mean hides a split personality.

🔬 Per-model takeaways

GLM-5.3-Flash — best configs

D-FP4L (nvidia GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local, NVFP4 QAD 1.0). The headline trade-off of the series so far: worst agent score in the GLM field (90.0±1.73 high / 91.0±1.00 max, 168/100 pts/hr, 260-min wall) and mid-pack prefill (2 009 t/s, TTFT@262k 134.9 s), but second-best long-context depth behaviour of all 15 configs (99.1% vs 100% Canada, ahead of fp8’s 93.9%) — the same NVFP4 format that collapses to 68.8% at 384k on stock vLLM holds 100% at 384k/480k here (see the depth post). The KV pool is 1,806,709 tokens (13-GiB fp8 pin, max_model_len 1,047,552 restored; the native-mirror 7.2-GiB pin = 991,442 tokens caps context at 983,040 and scored 89 on one archived high run). Config mirrored glm53-native (port, batch settings, KV method) for a fair comparison; env/flags byte-verified against NVIDIA’s 2×DGX Spark recipe card.

DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 — reference row

Unchanged from the previous post: largest KV pool (3.6M), but 89.0±1.0 max (no reasoning_effort scaling), longest deep-context TTFT.

Bottom line

On 2×DGX Spark, T (technigmaai native TP2) remains the best all-rounder, G647 (TensorFold fp8) is the new production pick for agent work (best TF max score, fast decode, biggest TF KV pool, clean long-context Cyrillic behaviour), Canada W4A16 is the quality-safe slow lane (perfect depth score, half the decode speed), and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 still does not clear the bar (89 vs 92–96, no effort scaling). The new D-FP4L splits the verdict: skip it for agent throughput (last GLM row on pts/hr and wall time), but it is now the second-best long-context stack measured — NVIDIA’s QAD distillation removes the deep-context collapse that stock NVFP4 serving shows on the same format. Full per-depth Cyrillic results: see the quality post.

2. Depth quality degradation:

Summary

GLM-5.3-Flash: quality vs context depth — TensorFold DENSE fp8 vs q4 (2× DGX Spark) vs stock vLLM nvfp4 vs Canada W4A16 marlin vs NVIDIA FP4-Local QAD (eugr b12x) — Cyrillic (RU/UA) test

This is the previous Cyrillic depth-degradation post updated with the D-FP4L stack (nvidia’s official GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local, NVFP4 quantization-aware distillation 1.0, served on the eugr spark-vllm-docker b12x recipe, vLLM d20261015, KV 13 GiB fp8 → 1.81M-token pool). Measured with the identical harness. All five stacks’ rows come from the project’s PostgreSQL results database (1 133 task rows).

Setup. pset4-cyr = 6 exec-checked coding tasks + 4 exact-answer fact tasks + 2 needle-in-haystack tasks, wrapped in unique seeded Cyrillic filler. Prompts in RU and UA, 2 seeds (1000/1001), thinking disabled, temperature 0.7, max_tokens 1024. Depths: 8k / 64k / 192k / 384k / 480k prompt tokens; the 480k depth uses a reduced set (12 code / 4 fact / 4 needle, n=20 vs n=48 elsewhere). Metrics: code correctness (exec + assert), exact match on fact answers, finish_reason stop vs length (“cuts”), loop detector (≥8 repeats of a 40+ char line), contamination (raw special tokens in output). A full depth is 48 rows: 24 code / 16 fact / 8 needle.

Hardware. 2× DGX Spark (GB10, 128 GB unified each), TP2 over RoCE. All five stacks serve the same base model (GLM-5.3-Flash 320B/18B); the quantization differs per column: DENSE=fp8 (TensorFold), DENSE=q4 (TensorFold), stock vLLM NVFP4, W4A16 marlin (vLLM sm121), NVFP4-QAD (b12x).

Overall per-depth score (code+fact+needle): 8k — fp8 95.8 / q4 100.0 / vLLM 95.8 / Canada 100.0 / D-FP4L 95.8 %; 64k — 100.0 / 100.0 / 97.9 / 100.0 / 100.0; 192k — 100.0 / 89.6 / 87.5 / 100.0 / 100.0; 384k — 89.6 / 81.2 / 68.8 / 100.0 / 100.0; 480k — 70.0 / 80.0 / 75.0 / 100.0 / 100.0. Totals: fp8 199/212 (93.9%), q4 194/212 (91.5%), vLLM 183/212 (86.3%), Canada W4A16 212/212 (100.0%), D-FP4L 210/212 (99.1%). Contamination over all 212 rows: fp8 = 0, vLLM = 0, Canada = 0, D-FP4L = 0, q4 = 2 (stray special-token markers in code output at 384k and 480k; both tasks still passed exec — cosmetic).

Findings.

D-FP4L changes the NVFP4 story completely. Stock vLLM on the same NVFP4 format collapses in the fact lane exactly where the prompt gets deep: 11/16 at 192k, 3/16 at 384k, 0/4 at 480k — 29 cuts, of which only 10 recover with a 4096-token budget (19 genuine failures). NVIDIA’s QAD-distilled checkpoint of the same model, same format, same 2×DGX Spark TP2 geometry, scored 16/16 fact at every depth and 24/24 code at 64k–480k. Its single cut (one code task at 192k) recovered with max_tokens=4096 (finish=stop, passed) — a budget-bound miss, not degradation. Net: 0 genuine long-context failures across 212 tasks, loops 0, contamination 0.

Two caveats keep the celebration honest. First, D-FP4L’s only real misses are two short-context (8k) code tasks — the same miss count other stacks also show (fp8 22/24, vLLM 22/24), though the tasks only partially overlap: D-FP4L drops task #5 (both seeds), fp8 drops #1/#3, vLLM drops #3/#5. It is a shallow-context agentic weakness, consistent with its last-place agent score in the performance post (90.0 high), not a depth issue. Second, Canada W4A16 remains the only flawless row (100%, zero cuts) — but its decode trails D-FP4L by ~15% on the cold sweep (25.4 vs 29.2 avg t/s, flat-low 18–43 vs 25–42 t/s across the concurrency grid), and the ~2× decode cost only shows against the fp8/q4 rows (52.7–59.0 t/s). Offsetting that, D-FP4L holds a 1.81M-token KV pool vs Canada’s 1.34M.

Where this leaves the quant choice. The fp8-vs-q4 verdict stands (fp8 for the 192k–384k band and zero loops). The quality lanes are now three: W4A16 marlin — the perfection lane (100%, slowest decode); D-FP4L (NVFP4-QAD) — the new robustness/speed balance (99.1%, zero genuine depth failures, nvfp4-class speed, 1.81M pool); G647 fp8 — the throughput/balanced pick (93.9%, 52.7 t/s decode, 2.29M pool). The striking result is format-level: the NVFP4 collapse on deep Cyrillic context is a serving/checkpoint problem, not a format problem — QAD distillation removed what stock vLLM serving of the same format suffers (68.8% → 100% at 384k).

Limitation: single benchmark, 2 seeds, synthetic Cyrillic filler — not a full capability eval.

D-FP4L's sweep is clean too — 64/64, no re-measures needed; its 13-GiB KV pin (1.81M tokens, fp8) is the deepest pool outside the TensorFold/q4 and DSV4 rows.*

*TensorFold fp8 (G647) trades single-stream 4k-decode (31.8–55.8) for the strongest 0-depth c2/c4 decode (65.9–69.3 / 59.6–59.7). ## 🔬 Per-model takeaways

### GLM-5.3-Flash — best configs
**D-FP4L (nvidia GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local, NVFP4 QAD 1.0).** The headline trade-off of the series so far: worst agent score in the GLM field (90.0±1.73 high / 91.0±1.00 max, 168/100 pts/hr, 260-min wall) and mid-pack prefill (2 009 t/s, TTFT@262k 134.9 s), but **second-best long-context depth behaviour of all 15 configs (99.1% vs 100% Canada, ahead of fp8's 93.9%)** — the same NVFP4 format that collapses to 68.8% at 384k on stock vLLM holds 100% at 384k/480k here (see the depth post). The KV pool is 1,806,709 tokens (13-GiB fp8 pin, max_model_len 1,047,552 restored; the native-mirror 7.2-GiB pin = 991,442 tokens caps context at 983,040 and scored 89 on one archived high run). Config mirrored glm53-native (port, batch settings, KV method) for a fair comparison; env/flags byte-verified against NVIDIA's 2×DGX Spark recipe card.

### DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731 — reference row
Unchanged from the previous post: largest KV pool (3.6M), but 89.0±1.0 max (no reasoning_effort scaling), longest deep-context TTFT.

[details="Summary"]
# GLM-5.3-Flash: quality vs context depth — TensorFold DENSE fp8 vs q4 (2× DGX Spark) vs stock vLLM nvfp4 vs Canada W4A16 marlin vs NVIDIA FP4-Local QAD (eugr b12x) — Cyrillic (RU/UA) test
This is the previous Cyrillic depth-degradation post **updated with the D-FP4L stack** (nvidia's official GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local, NVFP4 quantization-aware distillation 1.0, served on the eugr spark-vllm-docker b12x recipe, vLLM d20261015, KV 13 GiB fp8 → 1.81M-token pool). Measured with the identical harness. All five stacks' rows come from the project's PostgreSQL results database (1 133 task rows).

**Setup.** `pset4-cyr` = 6 exec-checked coding tasks + 4 exact-answer fact tasks + 2 needle-in-haystack tasks, wrapped in unique seeded Cyrillic filler. Prompts in RU and UA, 2 seeds (1000/1001), thinking disabled, temperature 0.7, max_tokens 1024. Depths: 8k / 64k / 192k / 384k / 480k prompt tokens; the 480k depth uses a reduced set (12 code / 4 fact / 4 needle, n=20 vs n=48 elsewhere). Metrics: code correctness (exec + assert), exact match on fact answers, `finish_reason` stop vs length ("cuts"), loop detector (≥8 repeats of a 40+ char line), contamination (raw special tokens in output). A full depth is 48 rows: 24 code / 16 fact / 8 needle.

**Hardware.** 2× DGX Spark (GB10, 128 GB unified each), TP2 over RoCE. All five stacks serve the same base model (GLM-5.3-Flash 320B/18B); the quantization differs per column: `DENSE=fp8` (TensorFold), `DENSE=q4` (TensorFold), stock vLLM NVFP4, W4A16 marlin (vLLM sm121), NVFP4-QAD (b12x).

Overall per-depth score (code+fact+needle): 8k — fp8 95.8 / q4 100.0 / vLLM 95.8 / Canada 100.0 / **D-FP4L 95.8** %; 64k — 100.0 / 100.0 / 97.9 / 100.0 / **100.0**; 192k — 100.0 / 89.6 / 87.5 / 100.0 / **100.0**; 384k — 89.6 / 81.2 / 68.8 / 100.0 / **100.0**; 480k — 70.0 / 80.0 / 75.0 / 100.0 / **100.0**. Totals: **fp8 199/212 (93.9%)**, **q4 194/212 (91.5%)**, **vLLM 183/212 (86.3%)**, **Canada W4A16 212/212 (100.0%)**, **D-FP4L 210/212 (99.1%)**. Contamination over all 212 rows: fp8 = 0, vLLM = 0, Canada = 0, D-FP4L = 0, q4 = 2 (stray special-token markers in code output at 384k and 480k; both tasks still passed exec — cosmetic).

**Findings.**

**D-FP4L changes the NVFP4 story completely.** Stock vLLM on the same NVFP4 format collapses in the fact lane exactly where the prompt gets deep: 11/16 at 192k, 3/16 at 384k, 0/4 at 480k — 29 cuts, of which only 10 recover with a 4096-token budget (19 genuine failures). NVIDIA's QAD-distilled checkpoint of the same model, same format, same 2×DGX Spark TP2 geometry, scored 16/16 fact at every depth and 24/24 code at 64k–480k. Its single cut (one code task at 192k) recovered with `max_tokens=4096` (`finish=stop`, passed) — a budget-bound miss, not degradation. Net: **0 genuine long-context failures across 212 tasks**, loops 0, contamination 0.

Two caveats keep the celebration honest. First, D-FP4L's only real misses are two short-context (8k) code tasks — the same miss count other stacks also show (fp8 22/24, vLLM 22/24), though the tasks only partially overlap: D-FP4L drops task #5 (both seeds), fp8 drops #1/#3, vLLM drops #3/#5. It is a shallow-context agentic weakness, consistent with its last-place agent score in the performance post (90.0 high), not a depth issue. Second, Canada W4A16 remains the only flawless row (100%, zero cuts) — but its decode trails D-FP4L by ~15% on the cold sweep (25.4 vs 29.2 avg t/s, flat-low 18–43 vs 25–42 t/s across the concurrency grid), and the ~2× decode cost only shows against the fp8/q4 rows (52.7–59.0 t/s). Offsetting that, D-FP4L holds a 1.81M-token KV pool vs Canada's 1.34M.

**Where this leaves the quant choice.** The fp8-vs-q4 verdict stands (fp8 for the 192k–384k band and zero loops). The quality lanes are now three: **W4A16 marlin — the perfection lane** (100%, slowest decode); **D-FP4L (NVFP4-QAD) — the new robustness/speed balance** (99.1%, zero genuine depth failures, nvfp4-class speed, 1.81M pool); **G647 fp8 — the throughput/balanced pick** (93.9%, 52.7 t/s decode, 2.29M pool). The striking result is format-level: **the NVFP4 collapse on deep Cyrillic context is a serving/checkpoint problem, not a format problem** — QAD distillation removed what stock vLLM serving of the same format suffers (68.8% → 100% at 384k).

*Limitation: single benchmark, 2 seeds, synthetic Cyrillic filler — not a full capability eval.*
[/details]

As far as the outputs, at a glance they looked about the same, but inspecting them I just noticed little nuances missing for each line of output. They were relatively minor vs the speed boost, though, I guess. Then today I noticed that somehow it took English tags and output nothing but Chinese. Neat lol.

The problem is I have no idea what his different tagged images do. payload = {
        "model": model_name,
        "messages": [
            {"role": "system", "content": system_msg},
            {"role": "user", "content": user_msg}
        ],
        "temperature": 0.6,
        "reasoning_effort": "max",
        "top_p": 0.95,
        "stream": True


    }

As you can see, I set the top_p and the temperature, and reasoning effort (because entrpi defaults to no reasoning unless either you tell it to reason or just set the reasoning effort).

You might be quite right, though. Maybe it tweaks one of the other parameters by default. I think I used to set repetition penalty manually for Qwen 122B, but I stopped doing it for Entrpi because it never needed that. Maybe it just does it in the background.

My “harness” is just a python script with a loop that then goes back and checks the result against the model to see if it’s good.

ajvazan:

GitHub - kindlingai/glm-5.3-flash-exlr8-gx10: GLM-5.3-Flash exlr8 (EXL3-trellis experts) serving recipe for GB10: vLLM + mentat, TP=1/2/3/4, exlr8 MoE kernels · GitHub

Try this one GitHub - kindlingai/glm-5.3-flash-exlr8-gx10: GLM-5.3-Flash exlr8 (EXL3-trellis experts) serving recipe for GB10: vLLM + mentat, TP=1/2/3/4, exlr8 MoE kernels · GitHub stack.
My quality degradation test yielded one of the best results (all checks passed successfully, with the sole exception of one test case involving an 8k-token context window). Furthermore, the model performs very efficiently using standard settings (a batch size of 8192): it achieves approximately 2300 tokens per second during the “cold” prefill phase and 50 tokens per second during generation, with context lengths of up to 150k tokens (testing for other context sizes is still ongoing; the Spark chips are running at a clock speed of 2000 MHz).
This is a very intriguing quantization approach. It’s hard to believe that such a high degree of compression results in absolutely no issues. There must be some downside that inevitably arises from this kind of compression.

API_PORT=8002
SERVED_NAME=glm-5.3-flash

posts.cooked:
Latest test results, including EXLR8 for TP=2. It was surprise:

Summary

GLM-5.3-Flash exlr8 (EXL3-k3 experts over NVFP4) on 2× DGX Spark — 4.9M-token KV pool, 2 326 t/s prefill, 91.7 high / 91.0 max, 99.5 % depth quality

This adds one fully measured config to our GLM-5.3-Flash on-prem series on two DGX Spark GB10 boxes (2×128 GB unified, TP2 over RoCE): exlr8-k3 — kindlingai’s exlr8 recipe (EXL3-trellis 3-bpw routed+shared experts layered over the NVFP4 Flash base recipe, dense linears left FP8), served by the mmastrac/spark-glm53:v29 image. Same harness as every other row: tool-eval-bench 2.8.1.dev14, seed 42, hardmode, temperature 0, alpha 0.7, n=3 per reasoning effort; cold sweep 64 points 4 096→262 144 step 4 096 with unique seeded prompts. The Cyrillic depth-quality suite (pset4 / quant-depth — the same harness as the depth post) is included below: 211/212 (99.5 %).

Config card (verified from the image, not from the recipe name)

Item Value
Recipe kindlingai/glm-5.3-flash-exlr8-gx10 @ 6f5ede7 (base: the NVFP4 Flash recipe)

Engine vLLM 0.30.1rc1.dev193+gddd6fbca1 (mmastrac/vllm-openai nightly ddd6fbca + FlashKDA 17a037d + vllm#58720 routed-experts patch)
Executor mentatd 0.17.1 instead of Ray (/usr/local/bin/ray → mentatd; the engine’s distributed_executor_backend: “ray” is the mentat shim)

- **Quant verdict:** EXL3-trellis k3 experts + FP8 dense over an NVFP4 base is quality-neutral at high effort and +17 % decode versus the NVFP4 config of the same family, at 4.2× the KV capacity.
- **Depth quality:** **211/212 (99.5 %)** on the Cyrillic pset4 suite — 100 % at 64k/192k/384k/480k, zero cuts, zero loops; tied with DeepSeek-V4.1-TF and behind only Canada W4A16 (100 %), far ahead of the stock NVFP4 stack on the same base format (86.3 %, collapsing at 384k).
- Still not claimed: the spec-decode acceptance table — the `--spec-bench` section came back empty in this build's JSON.
*Limitation: n=3 per effort, one boot per measurement, 2 seeds and synthetic Cyrillic filler in the depth suite — not a full capability eval; tool-eval wall 142.6 min for the full 3 high + 3 max set.*
[/details]

posts.name: Johan Ekenberg
posts.cooked:
corbett_korbett:

Anyone else have the issue of GLM 5.3 flash barely reasoning despite its reasoning level being set to max? Not sure what im doing wrong

I had this and fixed it a week or two ago. Here is an agent summary of that situation with some links and helpful pointers:

You’re probably not doing anything wrong. Most GLM-5.3-Flash chat templates (the stock one, MiaAI’s, technigma’s default) put the effort hint at the very top of the prompt, as a system line like <|system|>Reasoning Effort: Max. On short prompts that works: low, high and max produce clearly different amounts of reasoning. In a long agent session, though, the line ends up tens of thousands of tokens back, and the model largely ignores it. Max then behaves like high, sometimes with almost no reasoning at all.

We measured it on our 2× Spark (84K-token history, same request, 4 runs):

  • line at the top: max = 11–528 reasoning tokens (about the same as high)
  • line moved to just before the final <|assistant|>: max = 1,900–7,000

Moving the line to the end has a second benefit: changing effort no longer invalidates the prefix cache. With the line at the top, every effort switch re-reads the whole prompt.

Fix: move the effort hint to the end of the prompt. strusty calls this effort_tail:
GLM-5.3-Flash NVFP4 on 3x DGX Spark, stock DGX OS: ~3,300 tok/s prefill, 3M-token KV, up to 64 concurrent requests (kindling TP=3) - #7 by stuart.trusty

One trade-off: at the end, the model obeys max on every turn, including routine tool-result turns, which reasoned about 5× more for us. We only add the line when the request ends with a user message.

If your low reasoning shows up specifically right after tool results, and at very long context, that’s a different issue. technigma documents it and fixes it with a template reminder:
glm-5.3-flash-gb10-tp2-native/docs/TOOL_REASONING_VALIDATION.md at main · technigmaai/glm-5.3-flash-gb10-tp2-native · GitHub

Checklist to give your agent:

  1. Render the exact prompt your server builds for a long-session request: apply the chat template with your request’s chat_template_kwargs, or log it. Find where the Reasoning Effort line sits.
  2. Compare usage.completion_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens at low, high and max, first on a short prompt, then on a long session history. If the levels separate on the short one but not the long one, it’s the placement issue.
  3. Split by whether the last message is a user message or a tool result. Only the tool-result case points to the second link.
  4. Also check that your client actually sends reasoning_effort and that the server doesn’t pin its own default.
  5. Fix: in the template, emit the effort line right before the final <|assistant|> instead of at the top, optionally only when the last message is from the user. Then repeat step 2.

posts.name: Azampatti
posts.cooked:
Same total parameters, same model. I just cut the Shared Experts in half.

For every token, the original model selects 8 of the 288 experts which will be ~18B parameters (Active Parameters). For each token, a new group is selected.

My Shared Experts cut those experts in half (4), and with the other active layers, it ends with ~12.5B Active parameters. Still, the “right token” is selected from a single expert, so in the case the Topk4 = the top4 out of the Topk8 that the model selected originally, the answer should be the exact same.

In my tests, 95% of the time by cutting the experts in half, you’ll get the same answer BUT I don’t leave it there. I re-train the Shared Experts to LEARN which are the right expert for each token for a variety of prompts (Coding, Math, knowledge, etc,etc). My Shared Experts learn from the original model and in the end, they choose the “correct” Top4 experts 99+% of the time.

In my tests (Coding, agentic, math, JSON, etc) I couldn’t distinguish the original from my model. I’m sure there will be tests on which mine will perform lower (i.e.: Certain Languages I haven’t trained on as I focused in English and now I’m adding Spanish as well), but for a dev, my models should be virtually the same but faster :)

Hope that clarifies.

Cheers!

posts.cooked:
Have made several new tests of the GLM 5.3F EXLR8 and DS 4.1F 1017:

  1. Real token-generation speed of GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on several langauges:
Summary

Real token-generation speed of GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on a 2× DGX Spark (GB10) TP2 pair

Both models were measured on identical hardware (2× GB10, tensor-parallel 2), with the same client, same prompt set and same measurement code: 132 streaming requests in the two short-context runs (66 per model) plus 53 long-dialogue requests (24 per model; DeepSeek retried behind a quiet gate), 6 languages, engine counters cross-checked against client-side timing.

TL;DR

  • Sustained single-stream decode is 53 tok/s on GLM-5.3-Flash and 66 tok/s on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (medians across 6 languages, thinking off, short context; DS re-measured in full on 2026-10-23 evening). The language spread is ±11% for GLM (47–59) and −6/+5% for DeepSeek (62–69).
  • Ukrainian is the slowest language on GLM (47.0 tok/s, 29.3% draft acceptance) and French the fastest (58.8 tok/s, 44.1%). On DeepSeek the ranking flips: Russian is fastest (69.1), German slowest of the six (62.3).
  • What a human actually perceives varies 2.4×: GLM emits 234 characters/s in English but 96 characters/s in Chinese, because tokenization density differs (4.64 vs 1.98 characters per token). Token rate is a hardware number; character rate is the user experience.
  • The 70–120 tok/s in your UI is a short-window artifact. The same model measures 70.7 tok/s over a 64-token answer and 54.9 tok/s over a 512-token answer. A speculative-decoding step emits 2–4 tokens in one SSE chunk every ~47 ms, so per-chunk windows swing between 40 and 160 tok/s while the average stays flat.
  • Default thinking costs 3–4.5 s before the first answer character: at effort = max GLM spends 169–256 reasoning tokens out of a 256-token budget, always in English; for French and Chinese the entire budget went to thinking and no answer character was emitted at all.
  • At 30–55k prompt tokens the two stacks converge: decode 41–60 tok/s (GLM) vs 38–55 (DS), while prefill stays flat at 2.2–2.4k tok/s on both — so a deep agent turn costs 13 s (30k) or 24 s (55k) of TTFT before the first token.
  • 4 concurrent streams: 26 tok/s per stream, 155 tok/s aggregate on GLM.

Test setup

GLM-5.3-Flash DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash
Hardware 2× DGX Spark GB10, TP2 (head spark2 + worker spark1) 2× DGX Spark GB10, TP2 (head spark3 + worker spark4)
Engine vLLM 0.30.1rc1.dev193 (mmastrac/spark-glm53:v29) + mentatd 0.17.1 TensorFold Zig build (tensorfold-dsv41-zig:pr65, display-KV)
Weights EXL3-trellis k3 experts + FP8/NVFP4 dense, DFlash2 drafter k=7 EXL3 ≈2.8 bpw (flash17 Zig pack, 203.8 GB)
Served id glm-5.3-flash on :8002 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-TF on :8002
Context limit 500 000 1 048 576

Client: plain Python stdlib SSE (urllib), temperature=0.6, stream_options.include_usage=true, ignore_eos=true with a fixed max_tokens window so every run decodes exactly the same number of tokens. Thinking is disabled with chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking=false unless stated otherwise.

Decode speed definition (the only one that is comparable across runs):

decode_tps = usage.completion_tokens / (t_last_chunk - t_first_token_chunk)

t_first_token_chunk is the first chunk carrying content or reasoning. This matters: the engine emits reasoning as delta.reasoning while LiteLLM renames it to reasoning_content; a probe that reads only one of the two keys starts the clock at the first content chunk, i.e. after the whole thinking block, and over-reports tok/s on thinking runs (we hit exactly this bug and fixed it).

Scenarios per language: short chat (64 tokens out), long answer (256), an agent-shaped dialogue with a tool result in context (1.1–2.2k prompt tokens, 256 out), and one run at the engine’s default thinking effort. 3 repetitions of the first three, 2 of the thinking run → 9 + 2 samples per language per model, 66 requests per model.

The boxes were verified idle (num_requests_running = 0 / requests_inflight = 0) before and after the runs. Two DeepSeek runs were discarded because their median inter-chunk latency was 69 ms and 72 ms against a 37.5 ms baseline — an external request from the workstation sharing that box (interleaved traffic, not the model).

Results — GLM-5.3-Flash

Language tok/s (median) min–max chars/s words/s chars/token draft acceptance tokens/step median ITL
English 53.4 43.2–58.2 234.4 40.4 4.64 40.4% 2.63 48.9 ms
Russian 54.2 52.2–56.0 183.0 35.7 3.46 39.9% 2.61 48.5 ms
Ukrainian 47.0 40.2–51.0 126.6 32.3 2.73 29.3% 2.13 45.4 ms
German 52.8 44.0–60.5 198.4 37.1 3.67 34.2% 2.44 46.4 ms
French 58.8 55.7–70.6 216.8 43.5 3.72 44.1% 2.95 48.6 ms
Chinese 48.1 43.5–54.3 96.0 n/a 1.98 31.6% 2.37 48.1 ms

Results — DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash

Language tok/s (median) min–max chars/s words/s chars/token tokens/round median ITL
English 67.5 60.9–80.9 260.9 48.8 3.68 2.75 39.3 ms
Russian 69.1 60.0–77.2 199.3 44.0 3.06 2.56 37.3 ms
Ukrainian 63.5 59.6–65.0 161.4 39.5 2.56 2.31 35.9 ms
German 62.3 58.3–72.0 219.7 42.7 3.52 2.37 35.7 ms
French 68.3 59.6–76.9 227.9 47.9 3.35 2.69 37.8 ms
Chinese 64.6 64.2–75.8 121.3 n/a 1.83 2.56 38.1 ms

The TensorFold engine does not export per-position draft acceptance; it exposes tensorfold_decode_rounds_total and tensorfold_completion_tokens_total, so the comparable figure is tokens per decode round (2.31–2.75, i.e. the same speculative-decoding class of speed-up as GLM’s 2.1–3.0 tokens per step).

Head to head

Language GLM tok/s DS tok/s DS/GLM GLM chars/s DS chars/s GLM s per 1000 chars DS s per 1000 chars
English 53.4 67.5 1.26× 234.4 260.9 4.3 3.8
Russian 54.2 69.1 1.27× 183.0 199.3 5.5 5.0
Ukrainian 47.0 63.5 1.35× 126.6 161.4 7.9 6.2
German 52.8 62.3 1.18× 198.4 219.7 5.0 4.5
French 58.8 68.3 1.16× 216.8 227.9 4.6 4.4
Chinese 48.1 64.6 1.34× 96.0 121.3 10.4 8.2

Characters per second are comparable only within a language: 1000 Chinese characters carry far more information than 1000 English characters, so the s/1000-chars column is meaningful as a GLM-vs-DeepSeek comparison inside one row, not across rows.

DeepSeek is 16–35% faster per token and 5–27% faster in characters per second on every language (largest on Ukrainian and Chinese, i.e. exactly where the GLM drafter is weakest). At 30–55k depth the advantage mostly disappears — see the long-dialogue table.

Why the language spread exists

Inter-chunk latency is not the problem: GLM steps every 45–49 ms in every language (DeepSeek every 35–39 ms). The difference is how many tokens each step yields:

  • GLM draft acceptance: French 44.1% (2.95 tok/step) → Ukrainian 29.3% (2.13) → Chinese 31.6% (2.37). The k=7 DFlash2 drafter is simply worse at predicting Ukrainian and Chinese continuations, so more decode rounds are needed per output token.
  • Tokenizer density then multiplies the effect: 4.64 characters per token in English vs 2.73 in Ukrainian and 1.98 in Chinese. Ukrainian text costs ~1.7× more tokens than English for the same message, at a lower token rate — hence ~126 chars/s vs 234 (table rounds to 127).
  • DeepSeek shows the same mechanism with a much flatter profile (2.31–2.75 tok/round) and its fastest language is Russian, not English — a reminder that draft acceptance is a property of drafter + checkpoint + language, not of the hardware.

Thinking on (engine default effort)

Language GLM tok/s GLM chars/s reasoning tokens (of 256) est. time to 1st answer char DS tok/s DS wall (256 tok)
English 56.8 263.3 169 3.15 s 70.4 3.91 s
Russian 60.2 258.3 232 4.03 s 69.2 3.99 s
Ukrainian 56.8 256.4 242 4.43 s 66.4 4.19 s
German 58.4 264.1 221 3.96 s 65.2 4.21 s
French 60.7 275.9 256 4.39 s 71.2 3.88 s
Chinese 58.4 216.2 256 4.53 s 70.6 3.90 s

est. time to 1st answer char = TTFT + reasoning_tokens / tok/s (the engine does not timestamp the reasoning/content boundary, so this is an arithmetic estimate from counters, not a stopwatch reading).

Two things are worth flagging. First, GLM’s reasoning block is English in all six languages — that is why the thinking-phase speed (57–61 tok/s) looks better than Ukrainian or Chinese content generation (the 41–47% acceptance figure belongs to the earlier thinking-off runs, not to these thinking runs). Second, on a trivial question the default effort spends 169–256 reasoning tokens of a 256-token budget: 3.1–4.5 s before the first answer character, and in French and Chinese the whole budget went to thinking, so the answer never started inside the window. At enable_thinking=false the same question is answered in 0.6 s with 22 tokens. The DeepSeek engine does not report a reasoning-token split, but its total wall time shows the same behaviour.

Where the 70–120 tok/s in your UI comes from

Same model, same prompt, only the decode window length changes:

max_tokens median tok/s min–max
64 70.7 60.2–80.1
128 62.9 62.7–68.2
256 55.9 55.7–59.0
512 54.9 53.9–57.5

A 64-token answer measures 29% faster than a 512-token one, because the opening tokens are the ones the drafter predicts best. Agent traffic is dominated by short outputs (tool-call JSON, one-paragraph answers), so the number a UI samples is systematically the optimistic one. On top of that, a single speculative step delivers 2–4 tokens per SSE chunk; a client that samples per chunk or over sub-second windows sees 40–160 tok/s flicker around a 50–55 tok/s mean. Our per-second profile of a 512-token run: 30, 48, 50, 53, 48, 50, 45, 53, 53, 53, 28 tok/s — median 50.4, max 53.

Concurrency changes the picture in the other direction: 4 parallel streams on GLM give 25.8 tok/s per stream and 155 tok/s aggregate. If a dashboard shows one number above 100 tok/s sustained, it is almost certainly aggregate throughput or a held-burst gauge, not per-stream decode.

Long agent dialogues: 12 turns, 30k and 55k prompt tokens

Each dialogue is a 19-message SRE session — system prompt, six user/assistant pairs and six tool results carrying log payloads — sized with the engine’s own /tokenize (messages form) to 30 000 and 55 000 prompt tokens (±1%), with a unique salt per run so the prefix cache stays cold. The final question is answered inside the same fixed 256-token window, thinking off. GLM: 2 accepted runs per cell, 24/24 accepted. DeepSeek: cells combine pass 1 and the evening re-test, n is printed per cell.

Prefill is flat with depth and effectively identical on the two stacks — GLM 2 306–2 331 tok/s, DeepSeek 2 175–2 413 tok/s — so TTFT is 13 s at 30k and 24 s at 55k on both. For an agent turn that cost dominates everything decode does afterwards.

Decode, however, degrades very differently. GLM loses only 6–17% against its short-context medians and stays at 41–60 tok/s even at 55k (the one positive cell — English at 55k, +12% — is answer-content variance, not a depth speed-up). DeepSeek loses 16–39% and lands at 38–55 tok/s, the weakest cells being English — the language where its short-context lead was smallest. The short-context DeepSeek advantage (16–35% per token) therefore does not survive deep context: at 30–55k GLM is ahead on English, German and French while DeepSeek keeps the lead on Russian, Ukrainian and Chinese — a different ranking from the short-context table. GLM’s own language ranking is preserved at depth: Ukrainian and Chinese remain its slowest (41–44 tok/s), French the fastest (53–54 tok/s).

Practical consequence: one deep agent turn costs 13 s (30k) or 24 s (55k) of prefill before the first token, plus 5–6 s to stream a 256-token answer. Decode speed is no longer the differentiator at depth; TTFT and prompt length are.

Contamination note (DeepSeek). That box was concurrently serving a live coding agent during this phase (≈5 chat POST/min from the workstation, requests_inflight 0–2). A run was accepted only if (a) completion_tokens equalled the window, (b) median ITL was ≤1.25× the model baseline, (c) TTFT was ≤1.6× the expected value, and (d) the decode window was ≤1.25× chunks × median ITL — the last test catches a single hidden pause that a median cannot see (one French run showed a 2.9× ratio and 15.8 tok/s). 9 of 29 DeepSeek attempts were rejected on these grounds and retried behind a quiet-gate (requests_inflight == 0 for two consecutive polls) plus a full evening re-test of the contaminated cells with fresh salts (5/5 accepted first try, cold prefix cache); cells with a single accepted run are printed with n=1.

Caveats

  • Content differs across languages by construction (same semantic task, model-written answers), so part of the acceptance spread is content, not language. The Ukrainian and Chinese gap reproduced across all three scenarios and in an independent earlier session, but it is not a controlled minimal pair.
  • Medians of 9 runs per cell; min–max is given so the spread is visible. Single box per model, one quantisation per model — this compares two stacks, not two architectures.
  • The GLM stack is an EXL3-trellis k3 build, DeepSeek a 2.8 bpw EXL3 build; different engines, different drafter implementations.
  • ignore_eos forces full-length outputs, which is what makes runs comparable; real answers stop earlier and therefore measure higher (see the window-length table).
  • DeepSeek’s long-context cells were measured while that box also served a live coding agent: 9 of 29 attempts were rejected by the stall/ITL/TTFT rules, retried behind a quiet gate and re-measured in the evening with fresh salts (5/5 clean); five cells carry n=1. GLM’s 24 long-context runs were all clean.

lm-eval* reports bits_per_byte_stderr = N/A for these weighted aggregations, so the table above carries no error bars. I bootstrapped over documents from the per-sample log-likelihoods (2000 resamples, seed 0) to get the doc-level uncertainty:*

Consequences:

  • WikiText does not support a ranking of those three models.* With 62 documents the doc-level scatter of BPB itself is sd 0.020 (95 % CI ±0.04) — larger than the published gaps of 0.026 (EXL3 vs NVFP4) and 0.024 (NVFP4 vs DS4FV), and all three published values sit inside our interval. A paired comparison would be tighter (same documents, so per-doc difficulty cancels), but it needs per-document log-likelihoods from the other runs, which are not published. As things stand, the “best on English” ordering in post #48 is an ordering of point estimates, not an established ranking.*
  • UE Wiki Non-English (500 docs) separates only the NVFP4 row.* The gap to NVFP4 is 0.032 BPB — about 4× the doc-level scatter (sd 0.0074) — while the gap to the 4 bpw EXL3 checkpoint is 0.008 BPB, i.e. the size of the scatter itself. So: measurably better than NVFP4 on multilingual text, indistinguishable from 4 bpw EXL3.*
  • The task YAML does not pin a dataset revision, but the run resolved exactly these snapshots (from the local dataset cache): EleutherAI/wikitext_document_level @ 647234772b9554e208af6c826f23b99e3cac88c8, Jellyfish042/UncheatableEval-2026-07 @ 65889535d56aa38d448ce7e07b08e6e36c031545. Quote these with the numbers — a re-run against a newer snapshot is a different test.

Verification (numbers checked, not just printed)

  • Recomputed BPB independently from samples_.jsonl (verify_bpb.py, shipped with the run): UE −Σlogprob / (ln2 · bytes(target)) = 0.5080 — MATCH against the harness. WikiText needed doc['page'] bytes (its process_results counts the page, not the detokenized target) = 0.3764 — MATCH; using target bytes instead gives 0.3915, i.e. 4 % higher, which is a definition artefact, not a harness bug.**
  • Request count reconciles**: the engine logged 599 POST /v1/completions from 192.168.1.23 in the run window, and the tokenizer predicts exactly 599 chunks (500 UE + 99 WikiText) — nothing extra, nothing missing.**
  • The client really talked to this engine**: system_fingerprint of the endpoint equals the one behind our glm-5.3-flash-tf alias.**
  • No proxy in the path.** Our LiteLLM front end rejects token-id prompts (Unmapped prompt format) and carries a fallback chain (glm-5.3-flash → DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017), so a proxied run can silently score a different model. Direct endpoint only.**

Why there is no DeepSeek row here

*We also serve DeepSeek‑V4.1‑Flash (2× DGX Spark, TensorFold Zig engine, :8002 on spark3). The same test cannot be run there: loglikelihood_rolling needs per-token prompt log-probabilities, and this engine returns none. Every request shape tried — logprobs: 1, logprobs: true, logprobs: 5, and echo + prompt_logprobs: 1, with both string prompts and token-id prompts — answered 200 with no logprobs block at all (no choices[].logprobs, no prompt_logprobs), i.e. the field is dropped, not computed.

This is by design, not a config knob: the server source refuses the field — engine/zig/zig/src/server/fields.zig documents “logprobs are refused (no engine reports them yet)” and returns logprobs are not supported by this model or backend (covered by the golden fixture tests/server/golden/errors/logprobs.json). The deployed pr65 build drops the field silently instead of refusing it, which is the same outcome for the harness. The Python TensorFold server gates the same request on the engine’s supports_logprobs capability (tensorfold/server/probabilities.py, probability_options(..., supported: bool = False)), and the recipe’s own divergence tool notes DSV4.1 runs with supported=False.

We deliberately did not substitute a teacher-forced scorer or a patched server to fill that row: a different pipeline is not comparable with harness numbers, and mixing the two would be the same mistake as comparing across tokenizers. Perplexity for DeepSeek on these engines is currently unavailable — for DS, quality has to be argued with tool-eval / long-context suites instead.

Honest limits

  • Our checkpoint is EXL3 k3 (3-bit), the table’s leader is 4 bpw — so the +0.56 %/+1.18 % gaps, where they are resolvable at all, are a quant-width statement, not an engine statement.
  • Bootstrap intervals cover document sampling only; they do not include run-to-run (batching, numerics) variance. Treat them as a floor on uncertainty.
  • The harness’s own WikiText task is a 62-document test set by construction; the 1–3.5 % byte-perplexity gaps the forum table reports can only be settled with a paired, per-document comparison, which is not published for those runs.
  • num_concurrent=4* does not affect BPB. max_length=4096 does — rolling chunks are scored without cross-chunk context — so it is held identical to post #48; a run with a different max_length is not comparable to this table.*
  • The DeepSeek statement above was verified against the deployed pr65 build and the current recipe tree; a future engine that starts reporting logprobs would change it.

Have made several new tests of the GLM 5.3F EXLR8 and DS 4.1F 1017:
1. Real token-generation speed of GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on several langauges:

[details="Summary"]
# Real token-generation speed of GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on a 2× DGX Spark (GB10) TP2 pair
Both models were measured on identical hardware (2× GB10, tensor-parallel 2), with the same client, same prompt set and same measurement code: 132 streaming requests in the two short-context runs (66 per model) plus 53 long-dialogue requests (24 per model; DeepSeek retried behind a quiet gate), 6 languages, engine counters cross-checked against client-side timing.

## TL;DR
- **Sustained single-stream decode is 53 tok/s on GLM-5.3-Flash and 66 tok/s on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash** (medians across 6 languages, thinking off, short context; DS re-measured in full on 2026-10-23 evening). The language spread is ±11% for GLM (47–59) and −6/+5% for DeepSeek (62–69).
- **Ukrainian is the slowest language on GLM** (47.0 tok/s, 29.3% draft acceptance) and **French the fastest** (58.8 tok/s, 44.1%). On DeepSeek the ranking flips: Russian is fastest (69.1), German slowest of the six (62.3).
- **What a human actually perceives varies 2.4×**: GLM emits 234 characters/s in English but 96 characters/s in Chinese, because tokenization density differs (4.64 vs 1.98 characters per token). Token rate is a hardware number; character rate is the user experience.
- **The 70–120 tok/s in your UI is a short-window artifact.** The same model measures 70.7 tok/s over a 64-token answer and 54.9 tok/s over a 512-token answer. A speculative-decoding step emits 2–4 tokens in one SSE chunk every ~47 ms, so per-chunk windows swing between 40 and 160 tok/s while the average stays flat.
- **Default thinking costs 3–4.5 s before the first answer character**: at effort = max GLM spends 169–256 reasoning tokens out of a 256-token budget, always in English; for French and Chinese the entire budget went to thinking and no answer character was emitted at all.
- **At 30–55k prompt tokens the two stacks converge**: decode 41–60 tok/s (GLM) vs 38–55 (DS), while prefill stays flat at 2.2–2.4k tok/s on both — so a deep agent turn costs 13 s (30k) or 24 s (55k) of TTFT before the first token.
- **4 concurrent streams**: 26 tok/s per stream, 155 tok/s aggregate on GLM.

## Test setup
|  | GLM-5.3-Flash | DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hardware | 2× DGX Spark GB10, TP2 (head spark2 + worker spark1) | 2× DGX Spark GB10, TP2 (head spark3 + worker spark4) |
| Engine | vLLM 0.30.1rc1.dev193 (mmastrac/spark-glm53:v29) + mentatd 0.17.1 | TensorFold Zig build (tensorfold-dsv41-zig:pr65, display-KV) |
| Weights | EXL3-trellis k3 experts + FP8/NVFP4 dense, DFlash2 drafter k=7 | EXL3 ≈2.8 bpw (flash17 Zig pack, 203.8 GB) |
| Served id | glm-5.3-flash on :8002 | DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-TF on :8002 |
| Context limit | 500 000 | 1 048 576 |

Client: plain Python stdlib SSE (`urllib`), `temperature=0.6`, `stream_options.include_usage=true`, `ignore_eos=true` with a fixed `max_tokens` window so every run decodes exactly the same number of tokens. Thinking is disabled with `chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking=false` unless stated otherwise.

**Decode speed definition** (the only one that is comparable across runs):

```plaintext
decode_tps = usage.completion_tokens / (t_last_chunk - t_first_token_chunk)

```
`t_first_token_chunk` is the first chunk carrying `content` **or** reasoning. This matters: the engine emits reasoning as `delta.reasoning` while LiteLLM renames it to `reasoning_content`; a probe that reads only one of the two keys starts the clock at the first *content* chunk, i.e. after the whole thinking block, and over-reports tok/s on thinking runs (we hit exactly this bug and fixed it).

Scenarios per language: short chat (64 tokens out), long answer (256), an agent-shaped dialogue with a tool result in context (1.1–2.2k prompt tokens, 256 out), and one run at the engine's default thinking effort. 3 repetitions of the first three, 2 of the thinking run → 9 + 2 samples per language per model, 66 requests per model.

The boxes were verified idle (`num_requests_running = 0` / `requests_inflight = 0`) before and after the runs. Two DeepSeek runs were discarded because their median inter-chunk latency was 69 ms and 72 ms against a 37.5 ms baseline — an external request from the workstation sharing that box (interleaved traffic, not the model).

## Results — GLM-5.3-Flash
| Language | tok/s (median) | min–max | chars/s | words/s | chars/token | draft acceptance | tokens/step | median ITL |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| English | 53.4 | 43.2–58.2 | 234.4 | 40.4 | 4.64 | 40.4% | 2.63 | 48.9 ms |
| Russian | 54.2 | 52.2–56.0 | 183.0 | 35.7 | 3.46 | 39.9% | 2.61 | 48.5 ms |
| Ukrainian | 47.0 | 40.2–51.0 | 126.6 | 32.3 | 2.73 | 29.3% | 2.13 | 45.4 ms |
| German | 52.8 | 44.0–60.5 | 198.4 | 37.1 | 3.67 | 34.2% | 2.44 | 46.4 ms |
| French | 58.8 | 55.7–70.6 | 216.8 | 43.5 | 3.72 | 44.1% | 2.95 | 48.6 ms |
| Chinese | 48.1 | 43.5–54.3 | 96.0 | n/a | 1.98 | 31.6% | 2.37 | 48.1 ms |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| English | 67.5 | 60.9–80.9 | 260.9 | 48.8 | 3.68 | 2.75 | 39.3 ms |

The TensorFold engine does not export per-position draft acceptance; it exposes `tensorfold_decode_rounds_total` and `tensorfold_completion_tokens_total`, so the comparable figure is **tokens per decode round** (2.31–2.75, i.e. the same speculative-decoding class of speed-up as GLM's 2.1–3.0 tokens per step).

## Head to head
| Language | GLM tok/s | DS tok/s | DS/GLM | GLM chars/s | DS chars/s | GLM s per 1000 chars | DS s per 1000 chars |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| English | 53.4 | 67.5 | 1.26× | 234.4 | 260.9 | 4.3 | 3.8 |
| Russian | 54.2 | 69.1 | 1.27× | 183.0 | 199.3 | 5.5 | 5.0 |
| Ukrainian | 47.0 | 63.5 | 1.35× | 126.6 | 161.4 | 7.9 | 6.2 |
| German | 52.8 | 62.3 | 1.18× | 198.4 | 219.7 | 5.0 | 4.5 |
| French | 58.8 | 68.3 | 1.16× | 216.8 | 227.9 | 4.6 | 4.4 |
| Chinese | 48.1 | 64.6 | 1.34× | 96.0 | 121.3 | 10.4 | 8.2 |

Characters per second are comparable only within a language: 1000 Chinese characters carry far more information than 1000 English characters, so the s/1000-chars column is meaningful as a GLM-vs-DeepSeek comparison inside one row, not across rows.

DeepSeek is 16–35% faster per token and 5–27% faster in characters per second on every language (largest on Ukrainian and Chinese, i.e. exactly where the GLM drafter is weakest). At 30–55k depth the advantage mostly disappears — see the long-dialogue table.

## Why the language spread exists
Inter-chunk latency is *not* the problem: GLM steps every 45–49 ms in every language (DeepSeek every 35–39 ms). The difference is how many tokens each step yields:

- GLM draft acceptance: French 44.1% (2.95 tok/step) → Ukrainian 29.3% (2.13) → Chinese 31.6% (2.37). The k=7 DFlash2 drafter is simply worse at predicting Ukrainian and Chinese continuations, so more decode rounds are needed per output token.
- Tokenizer density then multiplies the effect: 4.64 characters per token in English vs 2.73 in Ukrainian and 1.98 in Chinese. Ukrainian text costs ~1.7× more tokens than English for the same message, at a lower token rate — hence ~126 chars/s vs 234 (table rounds to 127).
- DeepSeek shows the same mechanism with a much flatter profile (2.31–2.75 tok/round) and its fastest language is Russian, not English — a reminder that draft acceptance is a property of drafter + checkpoint + language, not of the hardware.

## Thinking on (engine default effort)
| Language | GLM tok/s | GLM chars/s | reasoning tokens (of 256) | est. time to 1st answer char | DS tok/s | DS wall (256 tok) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| English | 56.8 | 263.3 | 169 | 3.15 s | 70.4 | 3.91 s |
| Russian | 60.2 | 258.3 | 232 | 4.03 s | 69.2 | 3.99 s |
| Ukrainian | 56.8 | 256.4 | 242 | 4.43 s | 66.4 | 4.19 s |
| German | 58.4 | 264.1 | 221 | 3.96 s | 65.2 | 4.21 s |
| French | 60.7 | 275.9 | 256 | 4.39 s | 71.2 | 3.88 s |
| Chinese | 58.4 | 216.2 | 256 | 4.53 s | 70.6 | 3.90 s |

`est. time to 1st answer char` = TTFT + reasoning_tokens / tok/s (the engine does not timestamp the reasoning/content boundary, so this is an arithmetic estimate from counters, not a stopwatch reading).

Two things are worth flagging. First, GLM's reasoning block is **English in all six languages** — that is why the thinking-phase speed (57–61 tok/s) looks better than Ukrainian or Chinese content generation (the 41–47% acceptance figure belongs to the earlier thinking-off runs, not to these thinking runs). Second, on a trivial question the default effort spends 169–256 reasoning tokens of a 256-token budget: 3.1–4.5 s before the first answer character, and in French and Chinese the whole budget went to thinking, so the answer never started inside the window. At `enable_thinking=false` the same question is answered in 0.6 s with 22 tokens. The DeepSeek engine does not report a reasoning-token split, but its total wall time shows the same behaviour.

## Where the 70–120 tok/s in your UI comes from
Same model, same prompt, only the decode window length changes:

| max_tokens | median tok/s | min–max |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 64 | 70.7 | 60.2–80.1 |
| 128 | 62.9 | 62.7–68.2 |
| 256 | 55.9 | 55.7–59.0 |
| 512 | 54.9 | 53.9–57.5 |

A 64-token answer measures 29% faster than a 512-token one, because the opening tokens are the ones the drafter predicts best. Agent traffic is dominated by short outputs (tool-call JSON, one-paragraph answers), so the number a UI samples is systematically the optimistic one. On top of that, a single speculative step delivers 2–4 tokens per SSE chunk; a client that samples per chunk or over sub-second windows sees 40–160 tok/s flicker around a 50–55 tok/s mean. Our per-second profile of a 512-token run: 30, 48, 50, 53, 48, 50, 45, 53, 53, 53, 28 tok/s — median 50.4, max 53.

Concurrency changes the picture in the other direction: 4 parallel streams on GLM give **25.8 tok/s per stream and 155 tok/s aggregate**. If a dashboard shows one number above 100 tok/s sustained, it is almost certainly aggregate throughput or a held-burst gauge, not per-stream decode.

## Long agent dialogues: 12 turns, 30k and 55k prompt tokens
Each dialogue is a 19-message SRE session — system prompt, six user/assistant pairs and six tool results carrying log payloads — sized with the engine's own `/tokenize` (messages form) to 30 000 and 55 000 prompt tokens (±1%), with a unique salt per run so the prefix cache stays cold. The final question is answered inside the same fixed 256-token window, thinking off. GLM: 2 accepted runs per cell, 24/24 accepted. DeepSeek: cells combine pass 1 and the evening re-test, n is printed per cell.

### GLM-5.3-Flash

| English | 55k | 55094 | 24.9 s | 2212 | 42.5 | -31.3% | 190 | 2 |

**Prefill is flat with depth and effectively identical on the two stacks** — GLM 2 306–2 331 tok/s, DeepSeek 2 175–2 413 tok/s — so TTFT is 13 s at 30k and 24 s at 55k on both. For an agent turn that cost dominates everything decode does afterwards.

**Decode, however, degrades very differently.** GLM loses only 6–17% against its short-context medians and stays at 41–60 tok/s even at 55k (the one positive cell — English at 55k, +12% — is answer-content variance, not a depth speed-up). DeepSeek loses 16–39% and lands at 38–55 tok/s, the weakest cells being English — the language where its short-context lead was smallest. The short-context DeepSeek advantage (16–35% per token) therefore does not survive deep context: at 30–55k GLM is ahead on English, German and French while DeepSeek keeps the lead on Russian, Ukrainian and Chinese — a different ranking from the short-context table. GLM's own language ranking is preserved at depth: Ukrainian and Chinese remain its slowest (41–44 tok/s), French the fastest (53–54 tok/s).

**Practical consequence:** one deep agent turn costs 13 s (30k) or 24 s (55k) of prefill before the first token, plus 5–6 s to stream a 256-token answer. Decode speed is no longer the differentiator at depth; TTFT and prompt length are.

**Contamination note (DeepSeek).** That box was concurrently serving a live coding agent during this phase (≈5 chat POST/min from the workstation, `requests_inflight` 0–2). A run was accepted only if (a) `completion_tokens` equalled the window, (b) median ITL was ≤1.25× the model baseline, (c) TTFT was ≤1.6× the expected value, and (d) the decode window was ≤1.25× `chunks × median ITL` — the last test catches a single hidden pause that a median cannot see (one French run showed a 2.9× ratio and 15.8 tok/s). 9 of 29 DeepSeek attempts were rejected on these grounds and retried behind a quiet-gate (`requests_inflight == 0` for two consecutive polls) plus a full evening re-test of the contaminated cells with fresh salts (5/5 accepted first try, cold prefix cache); cells with a single accepted run are printed with n=1.

## Caveats
- Content differs across languages by construction (same semantic task, model-written answers), so part of the acceptance spread is content, not language. The Ukrainian and Chinese gap reproduced across all three scenarios and in an independent earlier session, but it is not a controlled minimal pair.
- Medians of 9 runs per cell; min–max is given so the spread is visible. Single box per model, one quantisation per model — this compares two *stacks*, not two architectures.
- The GLM stack is an EXL3-trellis k3 build, DeepSeek a 2.8 bpw EXL3 build; different engines, different drafter implementations.
- `ignore_eos` forces full-length outputs, which is what makes runs comparable; real answers stop earlier and therefore measure higher (see the window-length table).
- DeepSeek's long-context cells were measured while that box also served a live coding agent: 9 of 29 attempts were rejected by the stall/ITL/TTFT rules, retried behind a quiet gate and re-measured in the evening with fresh salts (5/5 clean); five cells carry n=1. GLM's 24 long-context runs were all clean.
[/details]

2. GLM-5.3-Flash perplexity on 2× DGX Spark

[details="Summary"]
# GLM-5.3-Flash perplexity on 2× DGX Spark (EXL3 k3, kindlingai exlr8 recipe, v29 image): bits_per_byte vs the models in this thread
Reproducing the LM-evaluation-harness test from [post #48](https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/lets-optimize-nvidia-glm-5-3-flash-nvfp4-for-2x-dgx-spark/382939/48) on our serving stack, and one finding about the harness itself that changes how the numbers in that table should be read.

**Stack under test:** [kindlingai/glm-5.3-flash-exlr8-gx10](https://github.com/kindlingai/glm-5.3-flash-exlr8-gx10) recipe (`6f5ede7`), image `mmastrac/spark-glm53:v29` (vLLM `0.30.1rc1.dev193+gddd6fbca1`), **EXL3 k3** routed/shared experts (`VLLM_EXLR8_WIDTHS=k3`) over the NVFP4 checkpoint with dense FP8/NVFP4 projections, `kv_cache_dtype=fp8_e4m3`, TP=2 (head spark2 `.21`, worker spark1 `.19`), RoCE functions [1,3], `MAX_MODEL_LEN=500000`, `max_num_batched_tokens=8192`, `block_size=2304`, `AdaptiveKScheduler`, DFlash2 drafter (`num_speculative_tokens=7`), served id `glm-5.3-flash`, port 8002. Log-likelihood scoring takes prompt log-probs from the prefill forward pass with `max_tokens=1`, so the drafter and sampling settings cannot influence the BPB numbers below.

**Harness:** `lm-eval 0.4.13` (`lm_eval[api]` + `transformers` + `sentencepiece`, installed as a `uv tool`), client on a third node (spark3 `.23`) that does not host the GLM pair, so the client never competes with the server under test for CPU/RAM. Run window: **2026‑10‑24 00:19–00:28 EEST** (2026‑10‑23 21:19–21:28 UTC). The tokenizer is the served model's own — the copy the harness uses is byte-identical to the served `exlr8-release/tokenizer.json` (sha256 `19e773648cb4e65de8660ea6365e10acca112d42a854923df93db4a6f333a82d`), **not** a substitute.

```bash
lm-eval run --model local-completions \
  --model_args "model=glm-5.3-flash,base_url=http://192.168.1.21:8002/v1/completions,tokenizer_backend=huggingface,tokenizer=/home/admin/lm_eval_work/tokenizer-glm53,tokenized_requests=true,max_length=4096,num_concurrent=4" \
  --tasks uncheatable_eval_wikipedia_nonenglish,wikitext \
  --output_path ./results --log_samples

```
Whole datasets, no `--limit` (harness `n-samples` = 500 and 62, i.e. the full filtered test splits): 562 documents → **599 requests**, the exact chunk count predicted from the tokenizer (500 + 99), → **8 min 56 s** at `num_concurrent=4`, `max_length=4096`.

## Results
| Hugging Face model ID | UE Wiki Non-English BPB ↓ | WikiText BPB ↓ | byte PPL (UE / WT) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mia-AiLab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-TR3-4bpw (ID as listed in post #48) | 0.4999 | 0.3595 | 1.4141 / 1.2830 |
| [deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Vision-Exp) | 0.5054 | 0.4093 | 1.4195 / 1.3280 |
| [LibertAIDAI/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4](https://huggingface.co/LibertAIDAI/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4) | 0.5396 | 0.3856 | 1.4536 / 1.3064 |
| this stack — GLM-5.3-Flash EXL3 k3 (exlr8 recipe, v29 image, TP2) | 0.5080 | 0.3764 | 1.4221 / 1.2981 |

Gaps in byte perplexity (negative = better than that row): vs EXL3‑4bpw **+0.56 %** (UE) / **+1.18 %** (WT); vs DSv4‑Flash‑Vision‑Exp **+0.18 % / −2.26 %**; vs NVFP4 **−2.16 % / −0.64 %**.

Raw metrics from `results_.json`*: UE *`word_perplexity 28.6228`*, *`byte_perplexity 1.4221`*, *`bits_per_byte 0.5080`*; WikiText *`4.0349 / 1.2981 / 0.3764`*.*

## *The part that matters: how much of that table is resolvable*
`lm-eval`* reports *`bits_per_byte_stderr = N/A`* for these weighted aggregations, so the table above carries no error bars. I bootstrapped over documents from the per-sample log-likelihoods (2000 resamples, seed 0) to get the doc-level uncertainty:*

| task | docs | bytes scored | BPB | 95 % CI | sd |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| uncheatable_eval_wikipedia_nonenglish | 500 | 1,828,958 (target bytes) | 0.5080 | [0.4937, 0.5229] | 0.0074 |
| wikitext (wikitext-2-raw-v1 test) | 62 | 1,290,527 (page bytes) | 0.3764 | [0.3363, 0.4140] | 0.0199 |

*Consequences:*

- ***WikiText does not support a ranking of those three models.**** With 62 documents the doc-level scatter of BPB itself is sd 0.020 (95 % CI ±0.04) — larger than the published gaps of 0.026 (EXL3 vs NVFP4) and 0.024 (NVFP4 vs DS4FV), and all three published values sit inside our interval. A *paired* comparison would be tighter (same documents, so per-doc difficulty cancels), but it needs per-document log-likelihoods from the other runs, which are not published. As things stand, the "best on English" ordering in post #48 is an ordering of point estimates, not an established ranking.*
- ***UE Wiki Non-English (500 docs) separates only the NVFP4 row.**** The gap to NVFP4 is 0.032 BPB — about 4× the doc-level scatter (sd 0.0074) — while the gap to the 4 bpw EXL3 checkpoint is 0.008 BPB, i.e. the size of the scatter itself. So: measurably better than NVFP4 on multilingual text, indistinguishable from 4 bpw EXL3.*
- *The task YAML does not pin a dataset revision, but the run resolved exactly these snapshots (from the local dataset cache): *`EleutherAI/wikitext_document_level`* @ *`647234772b9554e208af6c826f23b99e3cac88c8`*, *`Jellyfish042/UncheatableEval-2026-07`* @ *`65889535d56aa38d448ce7e07b08e6e36c031545`*. Quote these with the numbers — a re-run against a newer snapshot is a different test.*

## *Verification (numbers checked, not just printed)*
- *Recomputed BPB independently from *`samples_.jsonl`** (**`verify_bpb.py`**, shipped with the run): UE **`−Σlogprob / (ln2 · bytes(target))`** = 0.5080 — **`MATCH`** against the harness. WikiText needed **`doc['page']`** bytes (its **`process_results`** counts the page, not the detokenized target) = 0.3764 — **`MATCH`**; using target bytes instead gives 0.3915, i.e. 4 % higher, which is a definition artefact, not a harness bug.**
- Request count reconciles**: the engine logged 599 **`POST /v1/completions`** from **`192.168.1.23`** in the run window, and the tokenizer predicts exactly 599 chunks (500 UE + 99 WikiText) — nothing extra, nothing missing.**
- The client really talked to this engine**: **`system_fingerprint`** of the endpoint equals the one behind our **`glm-5.3-flash-tf`** alias.**
- No proxy in the path.** Our LiteLLM front end rejects token-id prompts (**`Unmapped prompt format`**) and carries a fallback chain (**`glm-5.3-flash → DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017`**), so a proxied run can silently score a different model. Direct endpoint only.**

## **Why there is no DeepSeek row here**
**We also serve DeepSeek‑V4.1‑Flash (2× DGX Spark, TensorFold Zig engine, **`:8002`** on spark3). The same test **cannot** be run there: **`loglikelihood_rolling`** needs per-token prompt log-probabilities, and this engine returns none. Every request shape tried — **`logprobs: 1`**, **`logprobs: true`**, **`logprobs: 5`**, and **`echo`** + **`prompt_logprobs: 1`**, with both string prompts and token-id prompts — answered **`200`** with **no `logprobs` block at all** (no *`choices[].logprobs`*, no *`prompt_logprobs`*), i.e. the field is dropped, not computed.*

*This is by design, not a config knob: the server source refuses the field — *`engine/zig/zig/src/server/fields.zig`* documents *"logprobs are refused (no engine reports them yet)"* and returns *`logprobs are not supported by this model or backend`* (covered by the golden fixture *`tests/server/golden/errors/logprobs.json`*). The deployed *`pr65`* build drops the field silently instead of refusing it, which is the same outcome for the harness. The Python TensorFold server gates the same request on the engine's *`supports_logprobs`* capability (*`tensorfold/server/probabilities.py`*, *`probability_options(..., supported: bool = False)`*), and the recipe's own divergence tool notes DSV4.1 runs with *`supported=False`*.*

*We deliberately did ****not**** substitute a teacher-forced scorer or a patched server to fill that row: a different pipeline is not comparable with harness numbers, and mixing the two would be the same mistake as comparing across tokenizers. Perplexity for DeepSeek on these engines is currently unavailable — for DS, quality has to be argued with tool-eval / long-context suites instead.*

## *Honest limits*
- *Our checkpoint is ****EXL3 k3 (3-bit)****, the table's leader is 4 bpw — so the +0.56 %/+1.18 % gaps, where they are resolvable at all, are a quant-width statement, not an engine statement.*
- *Bootstrap intervals cover document sampling only; they do not include run-to-run (batching, numerics) variance. Treat them as a floor on uncertainty.*
- *The harness's own WikiText task is a 62-document test set by construction; the 1–3.5 % byte-perplexity gaps the forum table reports can only be settled with a paired, per-document comparison, which is not published for those runs.*
- `num_concurrent=4`* does not affect BPB. *`max_length=4096`* ****does**** — rolling chunks are scored without cross-chunk context — so it is held identical to post #48; a run with a different *`max_length`* is not comparable to this table.*
- *The DeepSeek statement above was verified against the deployed *`pr65`* build and the current recipe tree; a future engine that starts reporting logprobs would change it.*
*Task definitions: *[uncheatable_eval](https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness/tree/main/lm_eval/tasks/uncheatable_eval)* · *[wikitext](https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness/tree/main/lm_eval/tasks/wikitext)* · harness: *[EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness](https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness)* · original UE project: *[Jellyfish042/uncheatable_eval](https://github.com/Jellyfish042/uncheatable_eval)
[/details]

TensorFold vs exlr8-k3 on 2× GX10: paired MRCR 8-needle test at ~400k context

I wanted to choose between the two stacks based on quality at the context lengths I actually use. I couldn’t find a long-context, thinking-on comparison, so I ran my own. Summary: on this test, TensorFold was clearly better: 18/34 fully correct vs 8/34, and the difference is statistically significant. Details follow so others can reproduce it or poke holes in it.

Hardware

2× ASUS GX10 (GB10, 128 GB each), TP=2 across the two nodes, ConnectX-7 direct link between them.

Stack A: TensorFold (Mia AI Lab recipe, v0.6.0)

  • GLM-5.3-Flash, DENSE=fp8 (changed from the default q4, since the model card names q4 dense as the main source of error), KV fp8
  • DFlash2 speculative decoding (k=7)
  • Spill tier enabled: SPILL_GIB=64 (this fixed the repeated huge prefills I got when kept prompt states were evicted)
  • TF_GLM_EFFORT_TAIL off, so the effort line sits where the stock template puts it
  • Nothing else changed from the recipe

Stack B: kindlingai exlr8 (mmastrac/spark-glm53:v29: vLLM 0.30.1rc1 + mentat 0.17.1)

  • k3 experts (3 bpw EXL3 trellis). k4 doesn’t fit at TP=2: vLLM has roughly 30 GiB of overhead on top of the weights.
  • TP=2 VLLM_EXLR8_WIDTHS=k3 MAX_MODEL_LEN=500000 KV_CACHE_MEMORY=26GiB, giving 4.24M KV tokens
  • DFlash2 drafter from the same directory as TensorFold
  • Setup note: node 2’s second CX7 port needed its own netplan (static IP, MTU 9000) before mentat would announce both rails
  • KV dtype and everything else at recipe defaults

On tool calling the two were tied: tool-eval-bench v2.8.1 scored 91/100 on both.

The test: OpenAI MRCR, 8-needle

openai/mrcr is a long multi-turn chat where the user asks for many pieces of writing, eight of which are near-identical requests. The final turn asks the model to reproduce, say, the 5th of those, starting with a random prefix. Grading uses OpenAI’s own method: 0 if the reply doesn’t start with the prefix, otherwise the difflib SequenceMatcher ratio against the correct answer. A score of 1.0 means the model tracked the right instance through about 400k tokens of distractors.

  • 34 samples, chosen by character count, all between 355k and 448k prompt tokens (median ~392k). Selection is seeded, so both stacks got exactly the same 34 prompts.
  • Thinking on, reasoning_effort=high (sent both as the request field and as chat_template_kwargs), temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, max_tokens 16384, one draw per sample
  • Run sequentially, one request at a time, with nothing else on the cluster
  • Script attached (mrcr_ab.py; the only dependency is pyarrow). It resumes after interruptions and includes the paired comparison.
python3 mrcr_ab.py run --base http://127.0.0.1:8010 --model glm-5.3-flash \
  --label tf-8n-400k --needles 8 --target-tokens 400000 --chars-per-token 4.8 --n 34
python3 mrcr_ab.py compare results-mrcr/tf-8n-400k.jsonl results-mrcr/exlr8-8n-400k.jsonl

Results

TensorFold (fp8 dense) exlr8 k3
Mean score 0.548 0.273
Fully correct (≥ 0.98) 18/34 8/34
Correct prefix 29/34 28/34
Hit max_tokens (cut) 4 5
Mean score excluding cuts 0.62 (n=30) 0.32 (n=29)
Median reasoning length 3.6k chars 5.9k chars
Median time per request 295 s 214 s

Per sample: both correct on 6, only TensorFold correct on 12, only exlr8 correct on 2.

Statistics

  • Paired difference in mean score (TF − exlr8): +0.276, 95% bootstrap CI [+0.099, +0.462] (10k resamples). The interval excludes 0.
  • Correct/incorrect, paired (exact McNemar on the 12 vs 2 discordant pairs): p = 0.013
  • Sign test on raw scores, with differences under 0.02 counted as ties: TF better 13, exlr8 better 5, ties 16, p = 0.096. This test is weaker because it throws away effect sizes and many pairs were both 0 or both 1.
  • Cuts don’t explain it: the gap is the same with cut samples excluded.

Interpretation and caveats

  • This compares stacks as shipped, not quants in isolation. Expert width (k3 vs 4-bit), dense precision, the KV/indexer implementation and the engine all differ, and I can’t say which one causes the gap.
  • It’s one long-context task, with one draw per sample at temperature 1.0. Samples within one run were sampled independently, but more draws per prompt would tighten the CI.
  • This doesn’t contradict the perplexity numbers in #920 (k3 within noise of Mia’s EXL3 4bpw on short text) or the depth test with thinking off. Those measure different things. MRCR at 400k with thinking on is the closest proxy I found for long agent sessions, and on that, TensorFold wins clearly.
  • exlr8 reasoned about 60% longer on the same prompts and still got fewer right, which looks like uncertainty rather than diligence.
  • exlr8 was faster per request at this depth (median 214 s vs 295 s).

I’m staying on TensorFold. I can share the raw jsonl for both runs if anyone wants per-sample scores.
